claims.source: A striking example in human communication concerns the perception of certain syllable sequences, such as an ambiguous syllable between /ga/ and /da/ preceded by either /al/ or /ar/. In both, the second syllable is physically identical, but is heard as /da/ or /ga/ depending on the preceding syllable (Lotto and Holt, 2006).
claims.evidence: This statement describes a known psychoacoustic phenomenon with citation.

claims.claim: The contextual effect on syllable perception still occurs if the preceding syllable is replaced by appropriately chosen tone sequences.
claims.source: Subsequent psychoacoustic investigations have revealed that this effect still occurs if the preceding syllable was replaced by appropriately chosen tone sequences, that it persists with substantial silent gaps between the two syllables, and that only very few tones are in fact necessary to bias the percepts one way or another (Holt, 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The contextual effect on syllable perception persists with substantial silent gaps between the two syllables.
claims.source: Subsequent psychoacoustic investigations have revealed that this effect still occurs if the preceding syllable was replaced by appropriately chosen tone sequences, that it persists with substantial silent gaps between the two syllables, and that only very few tones are in fact necessary to bias the percepts one way or another (Holt, 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Only very few tones are necessary to bias syllable percepts.
claims.source: Subsequent psychoacoustic investigations have revealed that this effect still occurs if the preceding syllable was replaced by appropriately chosen tone sequences, that it persists with substantial silent gaps between the two syllables, and that only very few tones are in fact necessary to bias the percepts one way or another (Holt, 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Contextual effects on syllable perception are likely not linguistic in nature, but reflect more basic adaptive neural mechanisms.
claims.source: Hence, these contextual effects are likely not linguistic in nature, but reflect more basic adaptive neural mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited psychoacoustic findings.

claims.claim: A sequence of two Shepard tones differing by half an octave can be perceived as ascending or descending in pitch.
claims.source: Here, we investigate the neural correlates of these contextual effects using a simplified paradigm, in which the context reliably biases the percept of an ambiguous acoustic stimulus: A sequence of two Shepard tones (Shepard, 1964), differing by half an octave in the frequencies of its constituent tones, can be perceived as ascending or descending in pitch.
claims.evidence: This describes the tritone paradox with citation.

claims.claim: The percept of Shepard tone pairs can be reliably manipulated by presenting a suitably chosen sequence of Shepard tones before.
claims.source: This percept can be reliably manipulated by presenting a suitably chosen sequence of Shepard tones before, setting up different contexts (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claims.claim: The contextual influence on Shepard tone perception is highly effective, rapidly established and can last for multiple seconds.
claims.source: This contextual influence is highly effective, rapidly established and can last for multiple seconds (Repp, 1997; Chambers and Pressnitzer, 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The ability to determine changes in pitch has relevance for distinguishing an approaching from a departing vehicle.
claims.source: Importantly, the ability to determine the changes in pitch has relevance for a wide spectrum of real-world tasks, ranging from distinguishing an approaching from a departing vehicle to distinguishing different emotions in human communication (Chebbi and Ben Jebara, 2018; Ethofer et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The ability to determine changes in pitch has relevance for distinguishing different emotions in human communication.
claims.source: Importantly, the ability to determine the changes in pitch has relevance for a wide spectrum of real-world tasks, ranging from distinguishing an approaching from a departing vehicle to distinguishing different emotions in human communication (Chebbi and Ben Jebara, 2018; Ethofer et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Shepard tones are acoustic complexes composed of octave-spaced pure-tones.
claims.source: Shepard tones are acoustic complexes, composed of octave-spaced pure-tones (top).
claims.evidence: Figure 1A shows the structure of Shepard tones.

claims.claim: Each Shepard tone is uniquely characterized by its base frequency fbase.
claims.source: Each Shepard tone is uniquely characterized by its base frequency fbase, and the difference between two Shepard tones by the difference of their base frequencies fdiff, usually given in semitones.
claims.evidence: Figure 1A describes the characterization of Shepard tones.

claims.claim: A Shepard tone shifted by a full octave projects onto itself and is therefore the physically same stimulus.
claims.source: A Shepard tone shifted by a full octave 'projects' onto itself, and is therefore the physically same stimulus.
claims.evidence: Figure 1A explains the circular nature of Shepard tones.

claims.claim: The space of Shepard tones forms a circle.
claims.source: The space of Shepard tones therefore forms a circle (bottom), in which each stimulus can be characterized as a so-called pitch class in semitones, which runs from 0 to 12, corresponding to a full octave.
claims.evidence: Figure 1A illustrates the circular pitch class space.

claims.claim: If the ambiguous Shepard pair is preceded with a sequence of Shepard tones with pitch classes above the first but below the second tone, listeners report an ascending percept.
claims.source: If the ambiguous Shepard pair is preceded with a sequence of Shepard tones with pitch classes above the first but below the second tone (red area), listeners report an ascending percept.
claims.evidence: Figure 1B describes the UP-Bias condition and its perceptual effect.

claims.claim: If the ambiguous Shepard pair is preceded by a sequence of Shepard tones with pitch classes below the first but above the second tone, listeners perceive a descending step.
claims.source: Conversely, if the ambiguous Shepard pair is preceded by a sequence of Shepard tones with pitch classes below the first, but above the second tone (blue area), listeners perceive a descending step.
claims.evidence: Figure 1B describes the DOWN-Bias condition and its perceptual effect.

claims.claim: Neural responses from individual neurons were collected in awake ferrets from the auditory cortex.
claims.source: Neural responses from individual neurons were collected in awake ferrets from the auditory cortex (left).
claims.evidence: Figure 1C describes the ferret recording methodology.

claims.claim: Individual neurons modulated their firing rate during the presentation of the stimulus sequence and exhibited tuned responses.
claims.source: Individual neurons modulated their firing rate during the presentation of the stimulus sequence and exhibited tuned responses (see Fig. S1).
claims.evidence: Figure 1C and reference to supplementary figure describe neural response properties.

claims.claim: Neural responses from populations of neurons in auditory cortex were collected from human subjects using MEG recordings.
claims.source: Using MEG recordings, we also collected neural responses from populations of neurons in auditory cortex from human subjects, performing the up/down discrimination task.
claims.evidence: Figure 1C describes the human MEG methodology.

claims.claim: The amplitude of the magnetic field was modulated as a function of time during the stimulus presentation.
claims.source: The amplitude of the magnetic field was modulated as a function of time during the stimulus presentation.
claims.evidence: Figure 1C describes the MEG signal characteristics.

claims.claim: Exposure to the contextual sequence resulted in localized adaptation that faded over the time-course of ~1 s.
claims.source: Exposure to the contextual sequence resulted in localized adaptation that faded over the time-course of ~1 s, consistent with stimulus specific adaptation (Ulanovsky et al., 2003) and with findings from a related human MEG study (Chambers et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section.

claims.claim: The localized adaptation is consistent with stimulus specific adaptation.
claims.source: Exposure to the contextual sequence resulted in localized adaptation that faded over the time-course of ~1 s, consistent with stimulus specific adaptation (Ulanovsky et al., 2003) and with findings from a related human MEG study (Chambers et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The finding is explicitly compared to SSA with citation.

claims.claim: The localized adaptation is consistent with findings from a related human MEG study.
claims.source: Exposure to the contextual sequence resulted in localized adaptation that faded over the time-course of ~1 s, consistent with stimulus specific adaptation (Ulanovsky et al., 2003) and with findings from a related human MEG study (Chambers et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The finding is explicitly compared to a human MEG study with citation.

claims.claim: Cells responding to pitch-changes are able to predict the context-sensitive percept of the tritone pairs.
claims.source: A straight-forward decoding approach demonstrates that the perceived pitch-change direction can be directly related to the contextually adapted activity of direction selective cells, that is cells that have a preference for sounds with ascending or descending frequency over time (Brosch and Schreiner, 2000; Brosch et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the decoding analysis.

claims.claim: Direction selective cells have a preference for sounds with ascending or descending frequency over time.
claims.source: A straight-forward decoding approach demonstrates that the perceived pitch-change direction can be directly related to the contextually adapted activity of direction selective cells, that is cells that have a preference for sounds with ascending or descending frequency over time (Brosch and Schreiner, 2000; Brosch et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This describes a known property of auditory cortical neurons with citations.

claims.claim: The neuronal adaptation dynamics are consistent with changes in neural activity in the auditory cortex estimated from human MEG recordings collected for the same sounds.
claims.source: These underlying neuronal adaptation dynamics are consistent with changes in neural activity in the auditory cortex estimated from human MEG recordings collected for the same sounds.
claims.evidence: This states consistency between ferret and human data.

claims.claim: A simplified model of cortical representation based on known properties of pitch-change selective cells accounts for the decoding effects.
claims.source: We can account for these effects in a simplified model of the cortical representation based on known properties of pitch-change selective cells, which matches both the results from the directional- and the distance-decoding analysis.
claims.evidence: This describes the modeling results.

claims.claim: The model is consistent with tuning changes and directional tuning of individual neurons.
claims.source: Further, the model is consistent with multiple observed properties of the neural representation, including tuning changes and directional tuning of individual neurons as well as the build-up of the contextual effect in humans.
claims.evidence: This describes properties the model accounts for.

claims.claim: The model is consistent with the build-up of the contextual effect in humans.
claims.source: Further, the model is consistent with multiple observed properties of the neural representation, including tuning changes and directional tuning of individual neurons as well as the build-up of the contextual effect in humans.
claims.evidence: This describes a property the model accounts for.

claims.claim: 662 responsive, tuned single units were collected from 7 awake ferrets.
claims.source: We collected neural recordings from 7 awake ferrets (662 responsive, tuned single units) and from 16 humans (MEG recordings) in response to sequences of Shepard tones (the 'Bias') followed by an ambiguous, semi-octave separated test pair (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the data collection.

claims.claim: MEG recordings were collected from 16 humans.
claims.source: We collected neural recordings from 7 awake ferrets (662 responsive, tuned single units) and from 16 humans (MEG recordings) in response to sequences of Shepard tones (the 'Bias') followed by an ambiguous, semi-octave separated test pair (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the data collection.

claims.claim: Human participants performed a two-alternative forced choice task, selecting between hearing an ascending or descending step in the test pair.
claims.source: The human participants performed a two-alternative forced choice task, selecting between hearing an ascending or descending step in the test pair, while ferrets listened passively.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental task for humans.

claims.claim: Ferrets listened passively during the recordings.
claims.source: The human participants performed a two-alternative forced choice task, selecting between hearing an ascending or descending step in the test pair, while ferrets listened passively.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental condition for ferrets.

claims.claim: The presence of the Bias reliably influences human perception towards hearing a pitch step bridging the location of the Bias.
claims.source: It has been previously shown (Chambers and Pressnitzer, 2014; Chambers et al., 2017) that the presence of the Bias reliably influences human perception, towards hearing a pitch step 'bridging' the location of the Bias, that is if the Bias is located above the first tone an ascending step is heard (Figure 1B middle), and a descending one, if it is below (Figure 1B bottom).
claims.evidence: This cites previous findings that motivate the current study.

claims.claim: During the presentation of the Bias sequence, the neural response adapts over time for individual cells.
claims.source: During the presentation of the Bias sequence (10 tones, black bars), the neural response adapts over time (individual cell). This adaptation occurs for all parts of the response, shown here is the onset part (0–50ms, black).
claims.evidence: Figure 2A1 shows adaptation in an individual cell.

claims.claim: On the population level, the response reaches an adapted plateau 13% below the initial response after about 5 stimuli.
claims.source: On the population level, the response reaches an adapted plateau 13% below the initial response after about 5 stimuli (τ=3.9 stimuli, also for the onset response).
claims.evidence: Figure 2A2 shows population-level adaptation.

claims.claim: The rate of reduction in neural response is similar to the rate of build-up of perceptual influence in human behavior.
claims.source: This rate of reduction is similar to the rate of build-up of perceptual influence in human behavior (Chambers and Pressnitzer, 2014; Chambers et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Figure 2A2 compares neural and behavioral timescales with citations.

claims.claim: After the Bias, the activity of cells is significantly more reduced around the center of the Bias compared to the edges.
claims.source: After the Bias the activity of the cells is significantly more reduced (Δ=33%, p=0.001) around the center or the Bias (<2.5 semitones from the center) compared to the edges (2.5–3 semitones from the center).
claims.evidence: Figure 2A3 shows localized adaptation with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Recovery of spontaneous neural firing rates from adaptation due to the Bias sequence progressed over multiple seconds with an exponential recovery time-constant of 1.2 s.
claims.source: Recovery of spontaneous neural firing rates from the adaptation due to the Bias sequence progressed over multiple seconds with an exponential recovery time-constant of 1.2 s.
claims.evidence: Figure 2A4 shows recovery dynamics.

claims.claim: In human auditory cortex, the Bias sequences evoked an adapting sequence of responses.
claims.source: In human auditory cortex the Bias sequences also evoked an adapting sequence of responses, here shown is the activity for a single subject (#8).
claims.evidence: Figure 2B1 shows adaptation in a human subject.

claims.claim: The adaptation of the neural response in humans proceeded with a similar time course as the single-unit response in ferrets and plateaus after about 3–4 stimuli.
claims.source: On average, the adaptation of the neural response proceeded with a similar time course as the single-unit response (A2), and plateaus after about 3–4 stimuli.
claims.evidence: Figure 2B2 shows population-level adaptation in humans.

claims.claim: Responses to probe tones in the same semi-octave as the Bias are significantly reduced (21%) compared to the opposite semi-octave.
claims.source: Responses to probe tones in the same (red) semi-octave are significantly reduced (21% for the first time window, signed ranks test, p<0.0001) compared to the corresponding response in the opposite semi-octave (blue), indicating a local effect of adaptation.
claims.evidence: Figure 2B3 shows localized adaptation in human MEG with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Most cells exhibited an onset type tuning with a brief response within the first 50ms after stimulus onset.
claims.source: Most cells exhibited an onset type tuning, that is a brief response within the first 50ms (orange) each after stimulus onset, but no sustained (red, 50–100ms) or offset response (black, 0–50ms in the silence after the stimulus).
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A describes onset-type neurons.

claims.claim: Onset-type cells typically showed broad/complex tuning with respect to the pitch class of the stimulus.
claims.source: These cells typically showed broad/complex tuning w.r.t. to the pitch class of the stimulus.
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A describes tuning properties of onset cells.

claims.claim: A considerable fraction of cells had surprisingly sharp pitch class tuning, with tuning half-widths of only 2–3 semitones.
claims.source: A considerable fraction of cells had a surprisingly sharp pitch class tuning, with tuning half-widths of only 2–3 semitones, leading to comparably sparse response patterns.
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B describes sharply tuned neurons.

claims.claim: Sharply tuned cells often showed co-tuned onset and sustained responses.
claims.source: These cells often showed co-tuned onset and sustained responses.
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B describes response properties of sharply tuned cells.

claims.claim: Some cells exhibited predominant offset pitch class tunings with broad/complex tunings.
claims.source: The remaining cells exhibited predominant offset pitch class tunings, which showed similarly broad/complex tunings as the onset tuned cells.
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1C describes offset-type neurons.

claims.claim: Many cells were tuned narrowly enough to only be excited by a single constituent tone of the Shepard tone.
claims.source: This indicates that while many cells were tuned narrowly enough to only be excited by a single constituent tone, many others were excited and/or inhibited by multiple constituent tones of the Shepard tone.
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1E shows tuning halfwidth distribution.

claims.claim: Many cells were excited and/or inhibited by multiple constituent tones of the Shepard tone.
claims.source: This indicates that while many cells were tuned narrowly enough to only be excited by a single constituent tone, many others were excited and/or inhibited by multiple constituent tones of the Shepard tone.
claims.evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1E shows tuning halfwidth distribution.

claims.claim: Steps of less than 6 pitch classes lead to unambiguous percepts in unbiased Shepard pairs.
claims.source: In the case of an unbiased Shepard pair, steps of less than 6 pitch classes lead to unambiguous percepts, e.g. a 0st to 3st steps leads to an ascending percept (red) and a 0st to 9st (i.e. 0st = >-3st) step to a descending percept (blue).
claims.evidence: Figure 3A describes unambiguous percepts.

claims.claim: Semi-octave steps lead to an ambiguous percept which strongly depends on stimulus history.
claims.source: Semi-octave (0st to 6st, blue/red) steps lead to an ambiguous percept, which strongly depends on the stimulus history (Chambers et al., 2017; Chambers and Pressnitzer, 2014) and even the individual's specifics, such as language experience and vocal range (Deutsch, 1986).
claims.evidence: Figure 3A describes ambiguous percepts with citations.

claims.claim: The ambiguous percept depends on the individual's specifics, such as language experience and vocal range.
claims.source: Semi-octave (0st to 6st, blue/red) steps lead to an ambiguous percept, which strongly depends on the stimulus history (Chambers et al., 2017; Chambers and Pressnitzer, 2014) and even the individual's specifics, such as language experience and vocal range (Deutsch, 1986).
claims.evidence: Figure 3A describes factors affecting ambiguous percepts with citation.

claims.claim: The minimal distance hypothesis predicts the percept to follow the smaller of the two distances along the circle between the two pitch classes.
claims.source: This suggests the minimal distance hypothesis which predicts the percept to follow the smaller of the two distances along the circle between the two pitch classes
claims.evidence: Figure 3A describes the minimal distance hypothesis.

claims.claim: The population decoding shows that the distance between the Shepard tones is increased on the side of the UP-Bias, challenging the minimal distance hypothesis.
claims.source: However, the population decoding shows that the distance between the tones is indeed increased on the side of the UP-Bias, challenging the minimal distance hypothesis.
claims.evidence: Figure 3B shows the result that contradicts the minimal distance hypothesis.

claims.claim: The stimulus identity is reflected in the joint activity of all neurons.
claims.source: The stimulus identity (top) is reflected in the joint activity of all neurons (middle).
claims.evidence: Figure 4A illustrates the decoding approach.

claims.claim: The circular stimulus space of Shepard tones induces a circular manifold of responses in a lower dimensional space.
claims.source: If the neurons are considered as dimensions of a high-dimensional response space, the circular stimulus space of Shepard tones induces a circular manifold of responses, which lies in a lower dimensional space (light red plane).
claims.evidence: Figure 4A illustrates the dimensionality reduction concept.

claims.claim: The entire set of responses to 240 distinct Shepard tones is projected by the decoding into a low dimensional space where neighboring stimuli fall close to each other and form a circle.
claims.source: The entire set of responses to the 240 distinct Shepard tones (from the various Bias sequences) is projected by the decoding into a low dimensional space (dots, hue = true pitch class), in which neighboring stimuli fall close to each other and the stimuli overall form a circle.
claims.evidence: Figure 4B shows the circular decoding result.

claims.claim: If a stimulus was relatively above the Bias sequence, their representation is shifted to higher pitch classes.
claims.source: However, if a stimulus was relatively above the Bias sequence (△, bright, upward triangles), their representation is shifted to higher pitch classes, compared to the same stimulus when located relatively below the Bias sequence (▼, dark, downward triangles).
claims.evidence: Figure 4B shows repulsive shifts in decoded pitch class.

claims.claim: The preceding Bias repulsed the stimuli in the ambiguous pair in their represented pitch class.
claims.source: Hence, the preceding Bias repulsed the stimuli in the ambiguous pair in their represented pitch class.
claims.evidence: Figure 4B demonstrates repulsive effect.

claims.claim: Decoding of pitch class is reliable with r=0.995 correlation between real and estimated pitch classes.
claims.source: To demonstrate that decoding in this way is reliable, we compare real and estimated pitch classes (by taking the circular position in B) for each stimulus, which exhibits a reliable relation (r=0.995).
claims.evidence: Figure 4C shows the reliability of decoding.

claims.claim: After the Bias, the decoded pitch class is shifted from their actual pitch class away from the biased pitch class range with high significance (p<10–43).
claims.source: After the Bias the decoded pitch class is shifted from their actual pitch class away from the biased pitch class range with high significance (p<10–43, Wilcoxon-test).
claims.evidence: Figure 4D shows statistically significant repulsive shifts.

claims.claim: The size of the shift is influenced by the length of the Bias sequence.
claims.source: The size of the shift is influenced by the length of the Bias sequence (5 tones = red, 10 tones = black) and the time between the Bias and the test tones (τ=1.1 s).
claims.evidence: Figure 4E shows the effect of Bias length and time on shift magnitude.

claims.claim: The size of the shift is influenced by the time between the Bias and the test tones with a time constant of 1.1 s.
claims.source: The size of the shift is influenced by the length of the Bias sequence (5 tones = red, 10 tones = black) and the time between the Bias and the test tones (τ=1.1 s).
claims.evidence: Figure 4E shows temporal decay of the shift effect.

claims.claim: The weighted population decoder produces very similar results to the PCA decoder.
claims.source: As in Figure 3, the entire set of 240 distinct Shepard tones (from the various Bias sequences) is represented in a lower dimensional space (dots, hue = true pitch class), in which neighboring stimuli fall close to each other and the stimuli overall form a circle.
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows alternative decoding method with similar results.

claims.claim: The weighted population decoder explains >99% of the variance in pitch class estimation.
claims.source: As before for the dimensionality reduction decoding we compare real and estimated pitch classes (by taking the circular position in B) for each stimulus, which explains >99% of the variance.
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1C shows high accuracy of alternative decoder.

claims.claim: The Bias shifts the represented pitch class away with high significance (p<10^–43) in the population vector decoding.
claims.source: The influence of the Bias can be compared quantitatively, by centering the represented test stimuli around their actual pitch class and inspecting the difference between the two different Bias conditions. The Bias shifts them away with high significance (p<10^–43, Wilcoxon-test).
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1D shows statistical significance of repulsive effect.

claims.claim: The size of the shift in population vector decoding is influenced by the length of the Bias sequence with a time constant of 0.92 s.
claims.source: As before, the size of the shift is influenced by the length of the Bias sequence (5 tones = red, 10 tones = black) and the time between the Bias and the test tones (τ=0.92 s).
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1E shows temporal dynamics of the shift.

claims.claim: A stimulus elicits an activity distribution along the cochlea which is retained in shape on the intermediate level.
claims.source: A stimulus elicits an activity distribution along the cochlea (bottom) which is retained in shape on the intermediate level (2nd from below).
claims.evidence: Figure 5A illustrates the model architecture.

claims.claim: In the native state, the stimulus is transferred to the cortical level without adaptation.
claims.source: In the native state, the stimulus is transferred to the cortical level without adaptation (2nd from top, black) and integrated by the cortical neuron (top, black).
claims.evidence: Figure 5A illustrates the unadapted state in the model.

claims.claim: After a stimulus presentation, an adapted trough is left behind in the connections leading up to the cortical level.
claims.source: After a stimulus presentation, an adapted trough is left behind in the connections leading up to the cortical level (2nd from top, red), which reduces the cortical tuning curve locally.
claims.evidence: Figure 5A illustrates adaptation in the model.

claims.claim: Since tuning curves closer to the center adapt more strongly, the stimulus representation in the neural population shifts away from the region of adaptation.
claims.source: Since tuning curves closer to the center adapt more strongly, the stimulus representation in the neural population shifts away from the region of adaptation.
claims.evidence: Figure 5A explains the mechanism of repulsive shifts.

claims.claim: Applying the same analysis to the model leads to a circular decoding with estimated pitch classes of the Shepard pair shifted repulsively by the preceding Bias.
claims.source: Applying the same analysis as above (Figure 3) for the real data leads again to a circular decoding (B1), with the estimated pitch classes of the tones the Shepard pair shifted repulsively by the preceding Bias (B2, for more details see the description of Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Figure 5B shows model results matching data.

claims.claim: Single cells show adaptation of their responses colocalized with the biased region.
claims.source: Single cells show adaptation of their responses colocalized (different colors) with the biased region (colored bars, bottom). The Bias was presented in four different regions in separate trials, and the tuning of the cell probed in between the biasing stimuli.
claims.evidence: Figure 5C shows localized adaptation in individual cells.

claims.claim: Centered on the Bias, neurons in the auditory cortex adapt their response colocal with the Bias.
claims.source: Centered on the Bias, neurons in the auditory cortex adapt their response colocal with the Bias. The curves represent the difference in response rate between the unadapted tuning and the adapted tuning, again for model cells on the left and actual data on the right.
claims.evidence: Figure 5D shows population-level localized adaptation.

claims.claim: The presence of the Bias reduces the firing rate relative to the initial discharge rate by ~40% inside the Bias region.
claims.source: The presence of the Bias reduces the firing rate relative to the initial discharge rate, by ~40% (red), while the rate stays the same or is slightly elevated outside of the Bias regions (green)
claims.evidence: Figure 5E shows quantification of adaptation magnitude.

claims.claim: The firing rate stays the same or is slightly elevated outside of the Bias regions.
claims.source: The presence of the Bias reduces the firing rate relative to the initial discharge rate, by ~40% (red), while the rate stays the same or is slightly elevated outside of the Bias regions (green)
claims.evidence: Figure 5E shows specificity of adaptation.

claims.claim: If adaptation is assumed to be strictly local with no distributed activity, no change in stimulus representation is expected.
claims.source: The observed tuning curves could also be obtained if the adaptation was assumed to be strictly local, and no distributed activity in response to a stimulus was considered. In this case, however, no change in stimulus representation is expected (A2), below (red) and above (blue) curves are identical, since the local adaptation would reduce the response of each neuron (either multiplicatively or subtractively) and, hence, not changing the center of the represented stimulus.
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1A shows a model variant that doesn't produce repulsion.

claims.claim: If adaptation is assumed to be global across all inputs, tuning curves are predicted to scale rather than change in shape or position.
claims.source: The repulsive shifts in the represented stimulus could also be obtained, if adaptation was assumed to be global across all inputs, that is only on the postsynaptic side, determined by the total postsynaptic activity. In this case, however, tuning curves are predicted to scale, rather than change in shape or position (B1). This is inconsistent with the observed changes in tuning curve shape (Figure 5C–E).
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1B shows a model variant inconsistent with tuning curve data.

claims.claim: If local adaptation is combined with distributed activity in the ascending auditory system, sharply adapted tuning curves and repulsive influence are obtained.
claims.source: If local adaptation (either on the synaptic level or in the cells projecting on the present cell) is combined with a distributed activity in the ascending auditory system, sharply adapted tuning curves are obtained as well as a repulsive influence of a preceding sequence of Bias stimuli. In response to a stimulus, both local changes in tuning curves (C1) and Bias-repulsed stimulus representation are obtained (C2).
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1C shows the model that matches both encoding and decoding data.

claims.claim: The predicted directional percept is computed by the average over the cells' activity weighted by their directionality and their distance to the stimulus.
claims.source: The predicted directional percept D(S) for a stimulus S is computed by the average over the cells activity fi(S), weighted by their directionality Di and their distance to the stimulus wi.
claims.evidence: Figure 6A shows the directional decoding formula.

claims.claim: Predictions of directional percept depended on the length of the sequence and the predicted tone.
claims.source: Predictions depended on the length of the sequence (o=5 tones, •=10 tones) and the predicted tone (red = 1 st tone, blue = 2 nd tone).
claims.evidence: Figure 6C shows factors affecting prediction accuracy.

claims.claim: Predictive performance increased as a function of Bias length and distance to the Bias.
claims.source: Predictive performance increased as a function of Bias length and distance to the Bias, reflected as 1st (red) or 2nd (blue) tone after the Bias. Both dependencies are consistent with human performance and the build-up and recovery of adaptive processes.
claims.evidence: Figure 6D shows prediction accuracy as a function of experimental parameters.

claims.claim: For cells with BFs close to the pitch class of the test tones, the relative activities are significantly different (p=0.03) between ascending and descending preferring cells.
claims.source: For cells with BFs close to the pitch class of the test tones, the relative activities are significantly different (p=0.03, one-way ANOVA) between ascending and descending preferring cells, thus predicting the percept of these tones.
claims.evidence: Figure 6E shows statistically significant differential activity pattern.

claims.claim: In the absence of adaptation, no significant pattern emerges in the model.
claims.source: Applied to a population of model neurons (as in Figure 5, see Methods for details) subjected to the same stimulus as the real neurons, in the absence of adaptation (left) no significant pattern emerges.
claims.evidence: Figure 6F shows model results without adaptation.

claims.claim: If no directional cells are present in the model, adaptation leads to a distinct pattern for different relative spectral locations, but the lack of directional cells prevents a directional judgment.
claims.source: If no directional cells are present (middle), adaptation leads to a distinct pattern for different relative spectral locations, but the lack of directional cells prevents a directional judgment.
claims.evidence: Figure 6F shows model results without directional cells.

claims.claim: With adaptation and directional cells, a pattern of differential activation is obtained similar to the pattern in the neural data.
claims.source: Finally, with adaptation and directional cells a pattern of differential activation is obtained, similar to the pattern in the neural data.

results.result: The study collected single-unit recordings from 662 neurons in 7 awake ferrets and MEG recordings from 16 humans, using appropriate experimental protocols and equipment. Ferrets listened passively while humans performed a two-alternative forced choice task on ambiguous Shepard tone pairs.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C37-C38, C51-C54, and C111-C128 provide comprehensive methodological details including subject numbers, recording techniques, ethical approvals, and equipment specifications. The methods are well-documented with appropriate technical details for reproducibility.

results.result: Neural responses in both ferrets and humans showed localized adaptation to the contextual Bias sequence, with responses adapting over 3-5 stimuli and recovering with a time constant of ~1 second. This adaptation was significantly stronger (33% in ferrets, 21% in humans) within the Bias region compared to outside it.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C41-C43, and C56-C63 demonstrate consistent adaptation patterns across species with appropriate statistical tests (p=0.001 for ferrets, p<0.0001 for humans). The temporal dynamics match between single-unit and MEG data, and are consistent with cited SSA literature.

results.result: Auditory cortical neurons exhibited diverse response types including onset-type cells with broad tuning, sharply tuned cells (2-3 semitones halfwidth) with co-tuned onset/sustained responses, and offset-type cells. Many cells responded to single constituent tones while others integrated multiple octave-spaced components.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 describe the heterogeneity of neural response properties with supporting data from Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The characterization of tuning properties is well-documented and provides important context for understanding population responses.

results.result: Population decoding revealed that the Bias sequence repulsively shifted the represented pitch class of test tones away from the Bias region (p<10^-43), with shift magnitude depending on Bias length and temporal separation (τ=1.1s for PCA, τ=0.92s for population vector). This finding was robust across two independent decoding methods (PCA: r=0.995; population vector: >99% variance explained).
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C88 demonstrate a highly significant repulsive effect using rigorous decoding analyses. The consistency across two independent methods (PCA and population vector) and the extremely high statistical significance (p<10^-43) strongly support the finding. The temporal dynamics match adaptation recovery timescales.

results.result: The minimal distance hypothesis, which predicts percept based on the smaller circular distance between pitch classes, is contradicted by the neural data showing increased rather than decreased distance on the Bias side.
results.evaluation: Claims C74 and C10 clearly articulate and test the minimal distance hypothesis. The repulsive shifts demonstrated in C75-C88 directly contradict this hypothesis, providing strong evidence against a simple distance-based decoding mechanism.

results.result: A two-layer neural model with local adaptation at thalamo-cortical synapses and distributed input representation successfully accounts for both the repulsive shifts in population decoding and the localized changes in individual cell tuning curves (~40% reduction within Bias region). Alternative models with purely local or purely global adaptation fail to capture these dual properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C100 and C144-C146 present a mechanistic model that reconciles encoding and decoding observations. The model is well-constrained by data and explicitly tested against alternative mechanisms (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that local adaptation with distributed representation is necessary and sufficient.

results.result: A directional decoder based on pitch-direction selective cells successfully predicted the context-sensitive percept with 88-95% accuracy, with performance increasing as a function of Bias length and temporal proximity. Cells near the test tone showed significantly different activity (p=0.03) between ascending and descending preferring cells, and this pattern required both adaptation and directional selectivity in the model (p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C44-C45, and C101-C110 demonstrate that directional cells can predict perception with high accuracy. The model analysis (C106-C109) shows that both adaptation and directionality are necessary, with appropriate statistical support. The prediction accuracy and its dependence on experimental parameters match human psychophysical performance.

results.result: The neural model based on adapting pitch and pitch-direction cells accounts for multiple properties including directional decoding, distance-based decoding, tuning curve changes, and the temporal build-up of contextual effects in humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C48-C50 summarize the model's explanatory power. The model successfully integrates multiple experimental observations and makes testable predictions consistent with both ferret neurophysiology and human psychophysics.

results.result: The study concludes that contextual influences on perception may be encoded at the level of primary sensory cortices through basic neural response properties like adaptation and directional selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 represent the main conclusion, which is well-supported by the convergence of adaptation data, decoding results, and modeling. The mechanisms identified (SSA-like adaptation, directional selectivity) are indeed basic properties commonly found in primary sensory areas.

results.result: The neuronal adaptation dynamics in ferrets are consistent with changes in neural activity estimated from human MEG recordings under identical stimulus conditions.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 is supported by the parallel findings in C6-C7, C41-C43, and C56-C63, which show similar adaptation timescales and localization in both species. This cross-species validation strengthens the generalizability of the findings.

results.result: The introduction establishes that perception depends on stimulus context, that contextual effects occur across sensory modalities including audition, and that Shepard tone pairs provide a tractable paradigm for studying how context biases ambiguous pitch perception.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C30 provide appropriate background and motivation, all supported by relevant citations. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the study but do not constitute novel findings.

results.result: The study used Shepard tones (octave-spaced complex tones forming a circular pitch class space) in sequences where contextual Bias tones reliably influenced perception of ambiguous semi-octave test pairs. Stimulus parameters included 5 or 10 tone Bias sequences with varying temporal gaps and 32 different Bias configurations.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36, C55, C71-C73, and C129-C138 describe the stimulus design and psychophysical properties. These are well-documented methodological details supported by citations to prior work establishing the perceptual effects.

results.result: Data analysis included selection of 662 responsive neurons from 1467 recorded, classification of adaptation/facilitation using exponential fits, and population decoding using dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA and alternatives). Non-parametric statistics were used throughout.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C143 and C148 describe appropriate analysis methods with clear selection criteria and validation approaches. The use of multiple decoding methods and non-parametric statistics strengthens the robustness of the findings.

results.result: Neural responses in ferret auditory cortex and human MEG show localized adaptation to contextual Shepard tone sequences. The adaptation is frequency-specific, builds up over ~3-5 stimuli, reduces responses by 13-33% in the adapted region, and recovers with a time constant of ~1.2 seconds. This adaptation is consistent with stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA) and matches between ferret single-unit and human MEG recordings.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers accept these findings without challenge. The editor describes the data as 'convincing single-neuron data and analyses,' Reviewer 1 states 'experimental design and data collection appear to have been executed carefully,' and Reviewer 2 notes 'the methods seem sound and the conclusions warranted.' The consistency between ferret and human data strengthens the findings.

results.result: Decoding analysis using direction-selective cells successfully predicts the context-dependent percept of ambiguous tritone pairs. Cells with directional tuning (ascending vs. descending preference) show differential activity patterns that correlate with the perceptual bias induced by the contextual sequence, with statistical significance (p=0.03 for neural data, p<0.001 for model).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as a key finding. The editor notes the study 'demonstrates convincingly that traditional neural decoding models cannot explain percepts' and that the direction-aware approach provides an alternative. Reviewer 1 states 'the conclusion that traditional decoding models cannot explain the contextual effects on percepts is quite strong,' implicitly accepting the directional decoding results. Reviewer 2 calls the study 'elegant' and finds the case 'fairly convincing.'

results.result: Traditional pitch-class decoding based on minimal distance in circular Shepard tone space predicts the opposite of the actual percept. The neural representation shows repulsive shifts away from the biased region (p<10^-43), with stimuli above the bias shifted higher and stimuli below shifted lower, contradicting the minimal distance hypothesis.
results.evaluation: This negative result is strongly endorsed by reviewers. Reviewer 1 emphasizes 'the very convincing negative results' and states 'it demonstrates convincingly that traditional neural decoding models cannot explain percepts.' The editor similarly notes the manuscript 'demonstrates convincingly' the failure of traditional models. The statistical significance (p<10^-43) and consistency across decoding methods support this conclusion.

results.result: A two-layer feedforward model with local adaptation at synaptic connections and distributed spectral integration successfully reproduces both the repulsive shifts in pitch representation and the directional decoding effects. The model accounts for observed tuning curve changes, directional selectivity patterns, and the build-up of contextual effects in humans.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the modeling results as valid. Reviewer 1 notes 'subsequent analysis and modeling appear rigorous,' and Reviewer 2 states 'the methods seem sound and the conclusions warranted and carefully stated.' The model's ability to match multiple aspects of the data (tuning changes, directional effects, temporal dynamics) strengthens its credibility, though reviewers note uncertainty about whether it represents the actual mechanism (see below).

results.result: The authors conclude that contextual influences on perception may be encoded at the level of primary sensory cortices through basic neural response properties like adaptation and directional selectivity, rather than requiring higher-level cognitive processing.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express uncertainty about the broader implications. The editor notes 'the manuscript could be clearer on the wider implications,' and Reviewer 1 states 'beyond the very convincing negative results, it is less clear exactly what the conclusion is or what readers should take away from this study.' Reviewer 1 specifically asks 'does this study make predictions about how information from auditory cortex must be read out by downstream areas?' Reviewer 2 acknowledges this is 'an observational, rather than an interventional study, and therefore only able to identify plausible candidate mechanisms rather than making definitive identifications.'

results.result: Ferret auditory cortex neurons show diverse tuning properties to Shepard tones, including onset-type cells with broad tuning, sharply tuned cells (2-3 semitones halfwidth) with co-tuned onset and sustained responses, and offset-tuned cells. Many cells respond to single constituent tones while others integrate across multiple octave-spaced components.
results.evaluation: These characterization results are not specifically discussed by reviewers but fall under the general acceptance of the experimental methods. Reviewer 1 states 'experimental design and data collection appear to have been executed carefully,' and Reviewer 2 notes 'the methods seem sound.' The detailed characterization supports the subsequent decoding analyses.

results.result: The study collected single-unit recordings from 662 neurons in 7 awake ferrets and MEG recordings from 16 human subjects using carefully controlled Shepard tone sequences with systematic variation of bias length, timing, and pitch class. Humans performed a two-alternative forced choice task while ferrets listened passively.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the methodological approach without specific concerns. Reviewer 1 states 'experimental design and data collection appear to have been executed carefully. Subsequent analysis and modeling appear rigorous.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the methods seem sound' and 'I would rate the quality of this study as very high, and I do not have any major issues to raise.' The only minor suggestion is that 'it might be helpful to work a little bit more methods detail into the results section.'

results.result: Multiple decoding approaches (PCA-based dimensionality reduction and weighted population vector) produce consistent results showing circular organization of pitch class representation with high accuracy (r>0.995, >99% variance explained). The magnitude of repulsive shifts depends on bias length and decays with time constants of 0.92-1.1 seconds.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the decoding methodology. Reviewer 1 notes 'subsequent analysis and modeling appear rigorous,' and the consistency across multiple decoding methods strengthens the conclusions. The robustness testing with different dimensionality reduction techniques (including tSNE) supports the reliability of the findings.

results.result: Alternative model architectures without distributed activity or with only global adaptation fail to reproduce the observed repulsive shifts and tuning curve changes, demonstrating the necessity of local adaptation combined with distributed spectral integration.
results.evaluation: These control analyses are implicitly accepted as part of the rigorous modeling approach. Reviewer 1 states 'subsequent analysis and modeling appear rigorous,' and Reviewer 2 notes 'the methods seem sound.' The systematic comparison of model variants strengthens the mechanistic conclusions.

results.result: The model implementation used a sampling rate of 20 Hz, a population of 500 cells split equally among non-directional, upward-selective, and downward-selective cells, and non-parametric statistical tests throughout to avoid distributional assumptions.
results.evaluation: These technical details are accepted without comment as part of the overall sound methodology. Reviewer 1 notes 'subsequent analysis and modeling appear rigorous,' and Reviewer 2 states 'the methods seem sound.'
